 - $500
Is it true that, for every bipartite graph $G$, there exists some $\alpha\in [1,2)$ and $c>0$ such that\[\mathrm{ex}(n;G)\sim cn^\alpha?\]Must $\alpha$ be rational?
#713: [ErSi70,p.379][Er74c,p.78][Er75][Er78,p.30][Er81,p.30][ErSi84][Er91]
graph theory | 
turan number
A problem of Erdős and Simonovits. Erdős sometimes asked this in the weaker version with just\[\mathrm{ex}(n;G)\asymp n^{\alpha}.\]Erdős [Er67d] had initially conjectured that, for any bipartite graph $G$, $\mathrm{ex}(n;G)\sim cn^{\alpha}$ for some constant $c>0$ and $\alpha$ of the shape $1+\frac{1}{k}$ or $2-\frac{1}{k}$ for some integer $k\geq 2$. This was disproved by Erdős and Simonovits [ErSi70].
The analogous statement is not true for hypergraphs, as shown by Frankl and Füredi [FrFu87], who proved that if $G$ is the $5$-uniform hypergraph on $8$ vertices with edges $\{12346,12457,12358\}$ then $\mathrm{ex}(n;G)=o(n^5)$ but $\mathrm{ex}(n;G)\neq O(n^c)$ for any $c<5$.
A simplified proof was given by Füredi and Gerbner [FuGe21], who extended it to a counterexample for all $k\geq 5$. It remains open whether it is true for $k=3$ and $k=4$ (though Füredi and Gerbner conjecture it is not).
See also [571].

 The page's sentence about Frankl–Füredi cannot be right as stated, independently of what the source says. For a $k$-uniform $H$, $\mathrm{ex}(n;H) = o(n^k)$ forces $H$ to be $k$-partite, and Erdős's 1964 theorem then gives $\mathrm{ex}(n;H) = O(n^{k-c})$ for some $c > 0$. So no $k$-uniform hypergraph can satisfy both halves of "$\mathrm{ex}(n;G) = o(n^5)$ but $\mathrm{ex}(n;G) \neq O(n^c)$ for any $c < 5$".
And this particular $H = {12346, 12457, 12358}$ is 5-partite — for instance ${1}\ {2}\ {3,7}\ {4,8}\ {5,6}$ puts one vertex of each edge in each class.
The exponent should be 4 in both halves. Füredi–Gerbner (arXiv:1906.06657), Theorem 3.1, quoting Frankl–Füredi (JCTA 45 (1987) 226–262), state it as: "Let $H = {12346, 12457, 12358}$. Then $\mathrm{ex}5(n,H) = o(n^4)$ but $\mathrm{ex}5(n,H) \neq O(n^{4-\varepsilon})$ for any $\varepsilon > 0$."
The conjecture attribution on the page is correct — Füredi and Gerbner do write that they conjecture it for $k \in {3,4}$ as well.

 Your example does not work. This forbids a family of hypergraphs (if you merely forbid the one that corresponds to 3-APs, then taking all edges containing $1$ avoids this).
There are true single hypergraphs which avoid this. The original example was given by Frankl and Furedi, see https://arxiv.org/pdf/1906.06657 for further discussion.
